body:
In the 6.3 text we say:

> This section contains general requirements for the security of authentication mechanisms as well as setting out the different expectations for levels including requiring multi-factor for L2 and supporting hardware-based mechanisms for L3, such as standards provided by the Fast IDentity Online (FIDO) Alliance.

I think we need to clarify something fundamental here as I don't think we have properly done so up until now.

Which of the following two things are we saying here:

1) Your application must support MFA
2) You cannot allow users to use your application unless they have enabled MFA

I think we have been thinking along the lines of Option 2 whereas that seems completely unrealistic for L2. Maybe more realistic for L3.

If we assume that Option 1 is the correct interpretation then that changes how we consider the password requirements as password security will still be highly relevant at L2.

What do we think @elarlang @jmanico  @randomstuff @ryarmst ?

comments.body:
I don't get it, based on what you interpret that we require just MFA support but not the usage of MFA? (Also, how requiring supporting MFA without requiring using it makes sense?)

In this case we had previously and have also now, that ASVS level 2 for authentication requirements is the same as NIST AAL2.
* https://pages.nist.gov/800-63-4/sp800-63b.html#authentication-assurance-level-2

It is aligned with NIST SP 800-63B AAL2 and it is clear for me, that MFA is must have from L2.

So I think equating AAL2 to L2 was always a little theoretical and certainly we have not made an effort to do that this time around.

Do you think it is realistic or makes sense for an L2 app to enforce MFA on all users?

> Do you think it is realistic or makes sense for an L2 app to enforce MFA on all users?

Yes. Plus apply here many-years-to-live-with-that-standard time-window.

If something different is decided, we need to re-analyze quite many requirements and their levels in ASVS.

I understood that the requirement was intended to be "enforce the usage of MFA for all users".

My *very unpopular* personal opinion is that it may be overkill for some applications (let us say a Wordle-like for example) but that does not appear to reflect the consensus of the security crowd on the topic.

> I understood that the requirement was intended to be "enforce the usage of MFA for all users".

Just to be sure - based on issue title, the context here is L2, not ALL applications (from L1)

> the context here is L2, not ALL applications (from L1)

Yes, I intended to say "all users for L2+".

I agree that all L2 apps should require MFA. It's the right move to make when sensitive data is involved when is in alignment for L2/AAL2.

Perhaps loosening the SMS requirement may make this forced change more digestible.

I know this is bold, but passwords as a sole AuthN factor are dead and have been for some time.

Not only NIST but other standards & compliance frameworks in general are moving more and more to require some kind of MFA to be used everywhere, ASVS should reflect this for L2 which is most applications.

I do veer towards agreeing with @jmanico on considering loosening the SMS requirements - although it should be clearly discouraged still. E.g. financial sector in practice relies on SMS very broadly globally unfortunately, probably due to it being considered more suitable for people from all backgrounds who have never before used e.g. TOTP. They know it's less secure than TOTP, but still use it. Maybe in few years passkeys are actually so mature technology that it could be the real user friendly solution for this, but we're not there yet.

To argue a bit against myself and continue on the example, financial sector organizations also have robust risk management processes to also review & accept these sort of risks (using SMS) in a controlled way, and also put in place mitigating controls such as fraud detection technology. Which we cannot assume is not the case with most organizations.

But what is the problem to solve with SMS? It is kind of allowed for L2 and forbidden from L3.

| # | Description | Level | #v5.0.be |
| :---: | :--- | :---: | :---: |
| **6.6.1** | Verify that authentication mechanisms using the Public Switched Telephone Network (PSTN) to deliver One-time Passwords (OTPs) via phone or SMS are offered only when alternate stronger methods (such as push notifications) are also offered and when the service provides information on their security risks to users. For L3 applications, phone and SMS must not be available as options. | 2 | v5.0.be-2.7.1 |

> But what is the problem to solve with SMS? It is kind of allowed for L2 and forbidden from L3.

Agree, I don't see a problem here. In fact, I think this requirement is a clear example of requiring the app to provide the option at L2 but forcing it at L3. Which is kinda what I want to see for MFA in general.

I posted here because I think this is a fundamental question:
https://owasp.slack.com/archives/C06MNF14M/p1744187702739699

Important to note that enforcement is not possible on the app side, today, as the amr claim not is available to apps using IDPs like Entra ID or Google Identity Platform. Should that be ignored? Given how long the next version of ASVS will live, I believe it should.

Having discussed with Elar, requiring MFA enforcement is a big step but maybe we should be pushing this, as a forward looking standard. 

If we are going to require MFA enforcement, in the section text, we should recognise that this is a big step and maybe also be clear that if MFA is not being enforced at L2, a verifier should expect to see a clear set of mitigating controls.

The IdP question is also an interesting one that maybe we need to mention in section text.

I wonder about:

> requiring multi-factor for L2 and supporting hardware-based mechanisms for L3, such as standards provided by the Fast IDentity Online (FIDO) Alliance.

As far as I know, hardware tokens are more phishing resistant then MFA.  Will Level 3 require MFA when hardware tokens are in use? E.g: when Passwordless hardware tokens are used to authenticate a pin is required. This doesn't seem that clear to me, but this seems  in line with what NIST has published: https://www.nist.gov/document/election-security-series-multi-factor-authentication-fact-sheet

> I wonder about:
> 
> > requiring multi-factor for L2 and supporting hardware-based mechanisms for L3, such as standards provided by the Fast IDentity Online (FIDO) Alliance.
> 
> As far as I know, hardware tokens are more phishing resistant then MFA. Will Level 3 require MFA when hardware tokens are in use? E.g: when Passwordless hardware tokens are used to authenticate a pin is required. This doesn't seem that clear to me, but this seems in line with what NIST has published: https://www.nist.gov/document/election-security-series-multi-factor-authentication-fact-sheet

Not sure I understand your question

> Important to note that enforcement is not possible on the app side, today, as the amr claim not is available to apps using IDPs like Entra ID or Google Identity Platform. Should that be ignored? Given how long the next version of ASVS will live, I believe it should.

That is for sure important to note.

I don't think we should ignore it, but ask something like "if the strength or method of authentication is not verifiable from IdP, then it must be considered as single-factor and the application must require second factor verification". For example, authenticating the user via Gmail and then asking additionally TOTP via Google Authenticator.

> Not sure I understand your question

The question was:

>  Will ASVS Level 3 require MFA when hardware tokens are in use?

From what I understand, Level 3 is "requiring multi-factor" while "hardware-based mechanisms" only need to be supported. 
From  https://www.nist.gov/document/election-security-series-multi-factor-authentication-fact-sheet 

" a user could insert a physical **hardware token** (first factor) into the system and then type in a **memorized password** (second factor)"

So from that I gather that the intention is that Passwordless options not can be used without pin or biometry as a second factor in order to satisfy the Level 3 MFA requirement. At least, that is how I understand ASVS 5 as it it written at the moment. Was that the intention?

> I don't think we should ignore it, but ask something like "if the strength or method of authentication is not verifiable from IdP, then it must be considered as single-factor and the application must require second factor verification". For example, authenticating the user via Gmail and then asking additionally TOTP via Google Authenticator.

Requiring the application to check the amr claim, I like it!

> > I don't think we should ignore it, but ask something like "if the strength or method of authentication is not verifiable from IdP, then it must be considered as single-factor and the application must require second factor verification". For example, authenticating the user via Gmail and then asking additionally TOTP via Google Authenticator.
> 
> Requiring the application to check the amr claim, I like it!

We have it at the moment as OAuth-OIDC specific requirement:
* 10.5.5 Verify that, if specific authentication strength, methods, or recentness is required, the relying party (RP) verifies that the presented ID Token satisfies these constraints (using the 'acr', 'amr' and 'auth_time' claims respectively).

But I opened an issue (#2934) to make one abstract and more general requirement to address that.

> do you think we should be requiring hardware-based to be enforced at L3 or just require that it is supported?

Not sure whether you got my point here. What would be enforced, according to my understanding, when reading the NIST fact-sheet, is the use of  a **memorized password** (second factor) when **hardware token** (first factor) is used. If you are trying to align yourself to NIST understanding of MFA and the use of hardware tokens, then that is where you end up. . https://www.nist.gov/document/election-security-series-multi-factor-authentication-fact-sheet  

It could end up becoming quite confusing when implementing Passwordless authentication for apps while following ASVS 5.

So to move a bit forward here, what I would like to see is a proper clarification for Level 3 on the use of MFA and hardware tokens. Hardware tokens can be used both as a primary factor and as a multi-factor for authentication. Not all authenticators support this! see: https://www.w3.org/TR/webauthn-2/#sctn-authentication-factor-capability 

When hardware tokens are used as the primary factor, we should make it very clear whether a second factor (MFA) is required and give some advice regarding how that is normally done according to NIST, if that is the source you want to use. 

And yes, I believe it should be required for Level 3.

So I think the tasks to solve here are:

* Clarify in requirement whether MFA enforcement is required for L2
* Clarify in requirement whether single factor hardware based auth is sufficient for L3 or whether multi factor is still required
* Provide some context in section text.

In general, I think it would be worth waiting a few more days for more feedback

I would say hardware token single factor auth (to expand on the comment by @sydseter) should be allowed for L3, provided that the hardware token can **reliably** **attest** that it required PIN or biometrics as part of the authentication. I would considering adding to the text something like "_--, for example in WebAuthN by inspecting the attestation statement to see if UV flag is set._" to ensure the bar is set high enough.

Yes @ottosulin and then, as @elarlang mentioned on Slack
 
_Verify that security decisions based on threat analysis is documented in situations where multi-factor not is achievable or realistic and that compensating controls proportional to the perceived risk of compromise have been deployed._

The last part, is a suggestion from me to ensure that mitigations are in place so that the risk isn't just accepted regardless of the severity of the threat.

First, @sydseter or @tghosth  - please collect all the information from this issue about the L3-hardware-mfa topic and open a separate issue for that discussion. Let's keep this issue only for L2 and MFA enforcement discussion as the issue title says.

---

I try to conclude the discussion and the situation so far, and I just re-use my comment on ASVS slack channel from the related thread:

I would say, more or less, we have an agreement, forcing MFA is the way to go.

At the same time, we need to map and address the situations where it is not achievable, not realistic, or not reasonable. We need to address it one way or another in the ASVS.

In ASVS, we have some flexibility mechanisms:
* "Document your security decision based on your threat analysis" - we have used it, for example, for session management to be flexible with timeouts and max lifetime, because fixed values from NIST are not used in practice (let's say you can stay logged in in Gmail forever)
* In-requirement "split-levels" - in the same requirement, there is a different description for different levels, for example, a requirement from the OAuth chapter: "_Verify that the authorization code is short-lived. The maximum lifetime can be up to 10 minutes for L1 and L2 applications and up to 1 minute for L3 applications._"

If we want to leave the door open to not force MFA for level 2, then I think we need to use the first option - by default force MFA, otherwise you need to have a documented security decision for that, including how you monitor and defend against the usage of leaked passwords.

Sounds good. Still, a possibility for satisfying the mandatory MFA requirement by documenting security decisions may open the door for business interests to push back unwanted controls and accept risk simply in the interest of increasing cash-flow.
A good risk management strategy always includes a balance between acceptance, transfer and mitigation. If you leave this out, you will not achieve what you intend to do with having MFA as a mandatory requirement to be tested.
I have opened an issue here: https://github.com/OWASP/ASVS/issues/2970 regarding MFA and Level 3. Feel free to comment.

> Sounds good. Still, a possibility for satisfying the mandatory MFA requirement by documenting security decisions may open the door for business interests to push back unwanted controls and accept risk simply in the interest of increasing cash-flow. A good risk management strategy always includes a balance between acceptance, transfer and mitigation. If you leave this out, you will not achieve what you intend to do with having MFA as a mandatory requirement to be tested.

I'm ok with that. The message for using ASVS is that you should fork it and adapt to your own needs, but everything that is in ASVS is there for a reason. So if we have strong MFA enforcement or not, at the end it does not change much for those who are willing to ignore that security requirement.

With the documentation requirement "to keep the door open to not implement MFA" I actually intend to not make it easy - it's not that you just ignore the requirement, you need to prove what kind of alternative security requirements you have implemented and when analyzing how to achieve that you may figure out, that implementing MFA is better option than to implement alternatives.

This is the theory, now we need to translate into the form of requirement :)

In regards to your suggestion for an opt-out from session lengths and MFA authentication NIST also has the following stated: https://pages.nist.gov/800-63-FAQ/#q-8 

So as I commented in https://github.com/OWASP/ASVS/issues/2970#issuecomment-2805089646

The opt-out could be formulated for both Level 2 and 3, like this:

_Verify, in situations where authentication requirements not is achievable or realistic, by demonstrating comparability of any chosen alternative, to include any compensating controls, when the complete set of applicable requirements not is implemented._

or (to include the entirety of ASVS)...

_Verify, in situations where application security requirements not is achievable or realistic, by demonstrating comparability of any chosen alternative, to include any compensating controls, when the complete set of applicable requirements not is implemented._

So My suggestion is that we add the following under V15

15.2.5 | Verify, in situations where application security requirements not is achievable or realistic, by demonstrating comparability of any chosen alternative, to include any compensating controls, when the complete set of applicable requirements not is implemented. | 2

@sydseter this feels like a meta-requirement. Practically speaking, wherever a company is not complying with an ASVS requirement for someone reason, they will either need to accept non-compliance or provide a compelling explanation to the verifier.

A couple of times we have specifically provided for this in the requirement text. We did it recently and I can't remember where but I am sure @elarlang will remember immediately. I think this is what Elar is proposing in this case.

We currently say:

| # | Description | Level | #v5.0.be |
| :---: | :--- | :---: | :---: |
| **6.3.2** | Verify that the application requires users to either use a multi-factor authentication mechanism or a combination of single-factor authentication mechanisms. | 2 | v5.0.be-2.2.9 |

We could change this to:

| # | Description | Level | #v5.0.be |
| :---: | :--- | :---: | :---: |
| **6.3.2** | Verify that the application  requires users to either use a multi-factor mechanism or a combination of single-factor mechanisms to log in. Where this is considered impractical or it is considered a business necessity to allow authentication using a single-factor, the security decision and any mitigating controls should be clearly documented.  | 2 | v5.0.be-2.2.9 |

I do however prefer to either not mention the possibility at all and leave it to be explained like any other non-compliance or alternatively to explain in section text rather than the requirement.

What do people think?

There are certain areas where some flexibility might be in order. I believe authentication and session management fit this bill, but I would really hate for ASVS Level 2 and 3 to become so similar that you can't tell them apart. (E.g: All Idps, I can think of, support hardware-based authenticators.).
There is also little point in making MFA mandatory if the text it self allows for a complete avoidance of the requirement through acceptance alone. A good security risk management strategy is always to also ensure you mitigate and transfer the security risk as well, but in the interest of avoiding that each requirement becomes overly complex, I would say that you should either add a specific requirement that allows for some leeway through risk management like NIST does (https://pages.nist.gov/800-63-FAQ/#q-8), or, as you say, add this as a general section text when talking about the application security within the context of security architecture. And again, acceptance alone, in what ever form, in the interest of cash-flow or convenience, will always defy the purpose of having the requirement in the first place.

> A couple of times we have specifically provided for this in the requirement text. We did it recently and I can't remember where but I am sure @elarlang will remember immediately. I think this is what Elar is proposing in this case.

Probably you mean here session management requirements for session timeout and max lifetime. So the concept is - first we have a default requirement, with the possibility to have your own justification, but those must be reasonable and well-argued:
| # | Description | Level | #v5.0.be |
| :---: | :--- | :---: | :---: |
| **7.1.1** | Verify that the user's session inactivity period and maximum session lifetime before re-authentication are documented, appropriate in combination with other controls, and that documentation includes justification for any deviations from NIST SP 800-63B re-authentication requirements. | 2 | v5.0.be-1.3.1 |

And then we have implementation requirements to verify that it is implemented as documented:
| # | Description | Level | #v5.0.be |
| :---: | :--- | :---: | :---: |
| **7.3.1** | Verify that there is an inactivity timeout such that re-authentication is enforced according to risk analysis and documented security decisions. | 2 | v5.0.be-3.3.5 |
| **7.3.2** | Verify that there is an absolute maximum session lifetime such that re-authentication is enforced according to risk analysis and documented security decisions. | 2 | v5.0.be-3.3.2 |

---

> I do however prefer to either not mention the possibility at all and leave it to be explained like any other non-compliance or alternatively to explain in section text rather than the requirement.

Yes, I don't think this part should be in the requirement: "Where this is considered impractical or it is considered a business necessity to allow authentication using a single-factor, the security decision and any mitigating controls should be clearly documented."

I'll come back to the requirement wording with more fresh brain and to keep in mind my comment here: https://github.com/OWASP/ASVS/issues/2925#issuecomment-2805046334

I don't really want a separate documentation requirement for this. so I would suggest the following:

---

## V6.3 General Authentication Security

This section contains general requirements for the security of authentication mechanisms as well as setting out the different expectations for levels. In particular, enforcing the use of multi-factor authentication (MFA) is required for L2 and supporting hardware-based mechanisms (such as standards provided by the Fast IDentity Online (FIDO) Alliance) is required for L3.

Whilst this is a relatively aggressive stance on MFA, it is critical to raise the bar around this to protect users and any attempt to relax these requirements should be accompanied by a clear plan on how the risks around authentication will be mitigated, taking into account NIST's guidance and research on the topic.

Note that at time of release, NIST SP 800-63 considers email as [not acceptable](https://pages.nist.gov/800-63-FAQ/#q-b11) as an authentication mechanism ([archived copy](https://web.archive.org/web/20250330115328/https://pages.nist.gov/800-63-FAQ/#q-b11)).

The requirements in this section relate to a variety of sections of [NIST's Guidance](https://pages.nist.gov/800-63-3/sp800-63b.html), including: [§ 4.2.1](https://pages.nist.gov/800-63-3/sp800-63b.html#421-permitted-authenticator-types), [§ 4.3.1](https://pages.nist.gov/800-63-3/sp800-63b.html#431-permitted-authenticator-types), [§ 5.2.2](https://pages.nist.gov/800-63-3/sp800-63b.html#522-rate-limiting-throttling), and [§ 6.1.2](https://pages.nist.gov/800-63-3/sp800-63b.html#-612-post-enrollment-binding).

| # | Description | Level | #v5.0.be |
| :---: | :--- | :---: | :---: |
| **6.3.3** | Verify that either a multi-factor authentication mechanism or a combination of single-factor authentication mechanisms, must be used in order to access the application. If there is a critical business reason that requires relaxing this requirement, there must be a fully documented rationale and business case accompanied by a comprehensive set of mitigating controls. | 2 | v5.0.be-2.2.9 |
I love it!

The only thing I would add to this is that hardware-based authentication mechanisms should be required for Level 3, not just supported. I have updated https://github.com/OWASP/ASVS/issues/2970 to reflect my stance.

> The only thing I would add to this is that hardware-based authentication mechanisms should be required for Level 3, not just supported. I have updated [#2970](https://github.com/OWASP/ASVS/issues/2970) to reflect my stance.

This is a separate issue so let's discuss there.
@elarlang what do you think about this: https://github.com/OWASP/ASVS/issues/2925#issuecomment-2837645725

> [@elarlang](https://github.com/elarlang) what do you think about this: [#2925 (comment)](https://github.com/OWASP/ASVS/issues/2925#issuecomment-2837645725)

Maybe to make the 2nd part less wordy, for example:
> Verify that either a multi-factor authentication mechanism or a combination of single-factor authentication mechanisms, must be used in order to access the application. Relaxing this requirement requires a fully documented rationale and a comprehensive set of mitigating controls.

> My _very unpopular_ personal opinion is that it may be overkill for some applications (let us say a Wordle-like for example) but that does not appear to reflect the consensus of the security crowd on the topic.

A Wordle app does not need ASVS Level 2 verification, unless it wants you to guess the names of possible diseases it’s suspected that your friends might be suffering from.

> But what is the problem to solve with SMS? It is kind of allowed for L2 and forbidden from L3.
> 
> **6.6.1**	Verify that authentication mechanisms using the Public Switched Telephone Network (PSTN) to deliver One-time Passwords (OTPs) via phone or SMS are offered only when alternate stronger methods (such as push notifications) are also offered and when the service provides information on their security risks to users. For L3 applications, phone and SMS must not be available as options.	2	v5.0.be-2.7.1

The latest revision of NIST 800-63b (Revision 4, August 2024) states that SMS is classified as restricted; NIST reserves the right to tighten or revoke its use as threats evolve.

Also:

* Verifiers SHOULD look for carrier events like SIM swaps, number porting, abnormal device behavior, bind the number securely, etc., before sending a code. Extra diligence is required if you are going to use SMS for MFA since it's so weak
* Code lifetime: ≤ 10 minutes.
* A code is valid once only

So the part we are missing is the extra carrier events that verifiers are supposed to look for before trusting SMS - each time it's used. And in general, SMS is on the way out according to NIST 800-63b R4 so I think 6.6.1 is not going to age well.

Good point, I think it could be safer to refer to sms as a legacy authenticator, allowed given a fully documented rationale and a comprehensive set of mitigating controls. For L3 it makes sense to disallow the use of legacy authentication.

> Good point, I think it could be safer to refer to sms as a legacy authenticator, allowed given a fully documented rationale and a comprehensive set of mitigating controls. For L3 it makes sense to disallow the use of legacy authentication.

I like it and in direct alignment with NIST and where they are going. I'd also drop the push notification part for 6.6.1 since that's been determined to be weaker than SMS.  I would also suggest we add the carrier event verification to 6.6.1, something like:

_**6.6.1 Verify that PSTN-delivered OTPs (phone or SMS) are offered only alongside stronger options such as app-based TOTP/HOTP generators with clear risk disclosure to users, are prohibited for Level 3 applications, and that each single-use code expires within 10 minutes and is sent only after the verifier has securely bound the number, checked for high-risk carrier events (e.g., SIM swaps or porting), and applied heightened scrutiny due to the inherent weakness of SMS-based MFA.**_
I think from the "problem to solve" for this issue point of view, the SMS topic is off-topic here. To make discussions per topic followable, please open a separate issue for side topics.

> I think from the "problem to solve" for this issue point of view, the SMS topic is off-topic here. To make discussions per topic followable, please open a separate issue for side topics.

Agreed, I opened https://github.com/OWASP/ASVS/issues/3072 for 6.6.1 concerns
